clue.text: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia

definitions.text: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia

parts.words: Novel sort of attachment proposed by Moravia
parts.note: Alberto Moravia's novel L'amore coniugale names a married kind of love, read here as a sort of attachment

explanation.surface: An Italian novelist puts forward some unusual kind of emotional bond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new', but it is the book: Moravia's novel is translated as 'Conjugal Love'.
explanation.definitionFit: Conjugal describes the bond between husband and wife, a marital attachment.

clue.text: "Proud, fierce, jealous and irritable" Saxon

parts.note: Scott describes the Saxon thane of Rotherwood in Ivanhoe with these very words

explanation.surface: A quoted character sketch of a bad-tempered Anglo-Saxon.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Ivanhoe the hero's father, the Saxon lord of Rotherwood, is introduced as proud, fierce, jealous and irritable.
explanation.definitionFit: Cedric the Saxon is the irascible father figure in Walter Scott's Ivanhoe.

clue.text: Unbalanced vernal poet

indicators.note: unbalanced means disordered, so the letters of the next word are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: A springtime poet who has lost his mental balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unbalanced' rearranges VERNAL. Gérard de Nerval was a French Romantic poet who suffered bouts of madness, which makes the surface apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Gérard de Nerval was a nineteenth-century French Romantic writer of verse.

clue.text: Very widely distributed, like Pope's prayer

definitions.meaning: found everywhere, general across the whole world
Alexander Pope wrote a poem titled 'The ... Prayer'

explanation.surface: Something spread far and wide, like a pontiff's prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pope' suggests the head of the Catholic Church, but it is the poet Alexander Pope and his poem 'The Universal Prayer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something found everywhere is worldwide, and Pope's poem bears that adjective in its title.

clue.text: Scrupulous chap identified by Maugham and Eggleston

definitions.meaning: an upright person of strict integrity who keeps his word
Somerset Maugham's first play and a novel by the American Edward Eggleston share this title

explanation.surface: Two writers pick out a man of strict principles.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone of unbending integrity is a gentleman who keeps his word, and both writers used the phrase as a title.

clue.text: Poet showing connection between church and University Press, offered refusal to conform

parts.note: kirk is the Scottish word for a church
UP is the abbreviation for University Press

explanation.surface: A poet linked a church to a publisher and refused to fall in line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing connection between' is only a link joining the two pieces. The last phrase describes James Kirkup, who was a conscientious objector in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: James Kirkup was an English writer of verse and translator.

clue.text: Jones the architect says he's entering

definitions.text: Jones the architect says he's entering

parts.words: Jones the architect says he's entering
parts.note: the first name of the architect Jones, split into three words, is what someone says as he walks in

explanation.surface: An architect announces his arrival.
explanation.walkthrough: The architect is Inigo Jones; his first name split up reads 'in I go', what a man says on entering.
explanation.definitionFit: Inigo Jones was the seventeenth-century English architect of the Banqueting House.

clue.text: Royal and ancient pathway for novelist

parts.note: royal is read as 'King's', belonging to the king
a ley is a supposed prehistoric track aligning ancient sites

explanation.surface: A golfing phrase, Royal and Ancient, leads to a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal and ancient' recalls the St Andrews golf club; here 'Royal' gives KINGS and 'ancient pathway' gives LEY, a ley line.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley, author of The Water-Babies, and Kingsley Amis were both writers of fiction.

clue.text: Motion put forward at Oxford

parts.note: the Oxford Movement of the 1830s was nicknamed after one of its leaders, Edward Pusey

explanation.surface: A proposal tabled in a university debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Motion put forward' suggests a debating proposal, but it is a movement: the Oxford Movement, named after E. B. Pusey.
explanation.definitionFit: The High Church Tractarian revival was called after its leader, the Oxford theologian Pusey.

clue.text: Hardy officer found Garland withheld

parts.note: in Hardy's The Trumpet-Major the yeomanry officer Festus woos Anne Garland, who keeps herself from him

explanation.surface: A tough soldier discovers that a wreath has been held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective but is Thomas Hardy; 'Garland' is Anne Garland, heroine of The Trumpet-Major, who refuses the bragging yeoman Festus.
explanation.definitionFit: Festus Derriman is the boastful yeomanry officer in Thomas Hardy's novel The Trumpet-Major.

clue.text: Great literary figures like Gargantua and his son

definitions.meaning: towering writers, the titans of literature
Rabelais's Gargantua and his son Pantagruel are enormous beings

explanation.surface: Major writers compared to Rabelais's father and son.
explanation.definitionFit: Towering authors are called titans, and Rabelais's huge father and son are literally of colossal size.

clue.text: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918

definitions.text: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918

parts.words: What they all did for Sassoon in 1918
parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's poem of 1918 opens with the line that gives its title, about a whole crowd breaking into song

explanation.surface: A question about what a group did for a war poet at the Armistice.
explanation.definitionFit: Sassoon's poem celebrates a moment when every person burst into song.

clue.text: Likeness that is cover for little review

indicators.note: the letters for 'that is' go around, covering, the letters for the review

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
a mag is a short word for a magazine or review

explanation.surface: A portrait that serves as the cover picture of a small magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover for' looks like a magazine cover picture, but it is the container signal: the abbreviation for 'that is' wraps the short word for a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture or representation of someone is their likeness.

clue.text: Clearly like Kipling's In Black and White

definitions.text: like Kipling's In Black and White
definitions.meaning: something set down in black and white is made plain for all to see

explanation.surface: A remark that a Kipling story collection is plain to read.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's In Black and White is a story collection; 'in black and white' also means written out plainly.
explanation.definitionFit: Evidently and plainly are the same idea, as is a thing set out in black and white.

clue.text: He restarts, we review sad Moore chronicle

indicators.note: to review here is to go over again and reorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone begins again while we look over a sad tale by George Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' rearranges HE RESTARTS WE. George Moore's novel Esther Waters tells the hard life of a servant girl.
explanation.definitionFit: George Moore's novel of 1894 is a bleak story of a servant who bears an illegitimate child.

clue.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

definitions.text: From which Rex Warner's career took off?

parts.words: From which Rex Warner's career took off?
parts.note: Rex Warner's best-known novel of 1941 is named after a flying field, where planes take off

explanation.surface: A question about how a novelist's career was launched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took off' sounds like career success, but his novel is named for a place planes take off from.
explanation.definitionFit: An airfield where planes depart is the title of Rex Warner's 1941 novel.

clue.text: Beethoven song from South Australia

definitions.meaning: Beethoven set Matthisson's poem as a song with a woman's name for its title
the capital city of the state of South Australia

explanation.surface: A Beethoven song that comes from Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's well-known lied bears a woman's name, which is also that of South Australia's capital city.

clue.text: Bumper edition of The Waves?

parts.note: a huge printing of Virginia Woolf's novel is read as a set of enormous sea waves

explanation.surface: A large-format reissue of Virginia Woolf's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bumper edition' suggests a big book; enlarge the waves themselves and you get giant seismic sea surges.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant sea surges caused by earthquakes are the biggest waves of all.

clue.text: Sort of centuries-old historian led neurotics astray

indicators.note: astray means gone wrong, so the letters of the words before it go out of place

explanation.surface: An ancient historian leads a group of anxious people off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Astray' rearranges LED NEUROTICS. Aubrey de Sélincourt translated Herodotus, so he is a sort of centuries-old historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubrey de Sélincourt's Penguin translation of Herodotus made him the voice of an ancient chronicler.

clue.text: Last resort for Francesca

parts.note: Francesca's surname, da ..., is an Adriatic seaside town; her story ends there in death

explanation.surface: A woman with nowhere else to turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last resort' sounds like a final option, but it is a seaside resort, Dante's Francesca da Rimini.
explanation.definitionFit: Francesca da Rimini takes her name from the Italian Adriatic seaside town.

clue.text: Dickens's powerful schoolmaster?

parts.note: the kindly Canterbury headmaster in David Copperfield has a surname meaning powerful

explanation.surface: A forceful teacher created by Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Strong in David Copperfield is in fact gentle; the surname is what means powerful.
explanation.definitionFit: Powerful and mighty mean the same, and it is the surname of David Copperfield's headmaster.

clue.text: Position assumed by Miss Sobel

parts.note: Dava Sobel wrote a best-seller about John Harrison's search for a way to fix a ship's east-west location

explanation.surface: A stance taken by a woman named Sobel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position assumed' sounds like an attitude; it is a geographical coordinate, the title of Dava Sobel's book.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's east-west coordinate is one half of its location, and Sobel's book bears it as title.

clue.text: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)

definitions.text: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)

parts.words: "— them in feign'd camps to real arms" (Matthew Prior)
parts.note: the missing verb completes Prior's line about hardening soldiers through mock warfare

explanation.surface: A line of Matthew Prior with its first word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: To accustom or harden troops to war by practice is to habituate them.

clue.text: Purport of James Hanley and Alan Jenkins

definitions.meaning: the general meaning or gist of something

definitions.text: of James Hanley and Alan Jenkins
definitions.meaning: James Hanley wrote a novel and Alan Jenkins a book of poems with this one-word title

explanation.surface: The meaning of two writers' works.
explanation.definitionFit: The gist of what someone says is its general tenor, and the word is a title by both writers.

clue.text: A Morse foot

parts.note: the letter A in Morse code is dot then dash, short then long, which is the pattern of one metrical foot

explanation.surface: Inspector Morse's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Morse' is the letter A in Morse code, dot-dash: short then long, the pattern of a metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical foot of one short or unstressed syllable then one long or stressed syllable.

clue.text: Elizabeth Jolley's eponymous blonde

parts.note: Jolley's novel takes its title from a horse with a golden coat and pale mane

explanation.surface: The fair-haired heroine of an Elizabeth Jolley novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blonde' suggests a woman; it is a golden horse with a white mane, the title of Jolley's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden-coated horse with a cream mane, and the title of Elizabeth Jolley's 1980 novel.

clue.text: Strindberg season

parts.note: August Strindberg wrote a play named after a spring festival of the Christian year

explanation.surface: A theatre's run of Strindberg plays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strindberg season' sounds like a theatre festival; it is the season that names his play.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring Christian festival of the Resurrection, and the title of a Strindberg play.

clue.text: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)

definitions.text: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)

parts.words: "I could never … be angry with his judgment for not — with me" (T. Browne, Religio Medici)
parts.note: the missing word completes Browne's line about not resenting someone who holds a different opinion

explanation.surface: A quotation from Sir Thomas Browne with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharing someone's opinion is concurring, which Browne would not demand of others.
